Question:
If \(ab\ne0\) and \(|a|\ne|b|,\) the number of distinct values of \(x\) satisfying the equation

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{x-a}{b}+\frac{x-b}{a} &=\frac{b}{x-a}\\ &\quad+\frac{a}{x-b} \end{aligned} \]

is:
Solution:
Combining the fractions on each side reveals the same numerator. We must keep this numerator as a factor, since setting it equal to zero may give a solution.

The original equation requires \(x\ne a,b\). Also, the hypotheses give \(a\ne b\) and \(a+b\ne0\). Put \(N=(a+b)x-a^2-b^2\). The equation becomes
\[
\frac{N}{ab}=\frac{N}{(x-a)(x-b)}.
\]
For allowed values of \(x\), multiplying by the nonzero denominators gives
\[
N\bigl((x-a)(x-b)-ab\bigr)=0.
\]
Since \((x-a)(x-b)-ab=x(x-a-b)\), every solution must be among
\[
0,\qquad a+b,\qquad c=\frac{a^2+b^2}{a+b}.
\]
We now check that these are three different allowed values. The first two are distinct because \(a+b\ne0\), and neither equals \(a\) or \(b\), because \(a,b\ne0\). Also, \(c\ne0\), since \(a^2+b^2>0\). If \(c=a+b\), then \(a^2+b^2=(a+b)^2\), which would give \(2ab=0\), a contradiction. Finally,
\[
c-a=\frac{b(b-a)}{a+b},\qquad
c-b=\frac{a(a-b)}{a+b},
\]
so \(c\ne a,b\).

All transformations were equivalent on the original domain, so all three candidates satisfy the equation. There are \(\boxed{3}\) distinct solutions, choice \(\boxed{D}\).
